title: Cast Neurovascular Checks: Pain Out of Proportion Is a Warning
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After casting, worsening pain, paresthesia, pallor, coolness, weakness, delayed capillary refill, or increasing swelling can signal neurovascular compromise. Severe pain out of proportion or pain with passive stretch is an emergency cue.
recognize: Compare color, temperature, sensation, movement, capillary refill, swelling, and pain with the opposite limb when appropriate.
Numbness, weakness, increasing analgesic need, or inability to move digits is not routine post-cast discomfort.
priorities: Elevate as ordered when swelling is expected, reassess neurovascular status, and escalate concerning findings immediately.
Do not place objects inside the cast or ignore escalating pain because pulses are still present.
assessMonitor: Trend pain, sensation, motor function, perfusion, swelling, skin integrity, and cast fit.
interventions: Keep the cast dry, protect edges, reposition safely, and follow provider instructions for swelling and mobility.
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not be used to mask progressive neurovascular symptoms; reassess before and after pain medication.
teaching: Report increasing pain, numbness, swelling, odor, drainage, fever, or inability to move digits.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be delegated; interpretation of abnormal neurovascular findings and escalation remain licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Reassuring the patient because a distal pulse is present despite severe escalating pain and paresthesia.
oneLinePearl: A pulse does not rule out compartment syndrome.

title: Compartment Syndrome: Escalate Before Tissue Dies
bottomLine: Acute compartment syndrome is a limb-threatening emergency caused by rising pressure within a closed fascial space. Early recognition and urgent surgical evaluation matter more than waiting for late pulse loss.
recognize: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early high-risk findings.
Paresthesia, tense swelling, weakness, pallor, and pulselessness are progressively concerning; pulselessness is late.
priorities: Notify the RN/provider/emergency team immediately and maintain the limb at the ordered position without constrictive wrapping.
Do not delay escalation for repeated routine pain-medication trials.
assessMonitor: Serial neurovascular checks, pain trend, swelling, motor/sensory changes, and cast/dressing tightness.
interventions: Prepare for urgent evaluation and possible fasciotomy; loosen external constriction only if authorized by protocol/order.
medicationSafety: Analgesia is appropriate but cannot replace evaluation of disproportionate pain.
teaching: After injury or casting, worsening severe pain or numbness requires urgent assessment.
delegationScope: Recognition and escalation of suspected compartment syndrome are licensed-nurse responsibilities.
examTrap: Waiting for absent pulses before acting.
oneLinePearl: Compartment syndrome is diagnosed before the pulse disappears.

title: Hip Arthroplasty Precautions: Protect the New Joint
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: After hip arthroplasty, movement precautions depend on surgical approach and surgeon instructions. Use the prescribed approach-specific restrictions rather than teaching one universal set of hip precautions.
recognize: Sudden severe hip pain, shortening, abnormal rotation, or inability to bear weight can suggest dislocation.
Posterior and anterior surgical approaches may have different prohibited movements.
priorities: Follow the documented postoperative precautions and safe-transfer plan exactly.
Escalate suspected dislocation or acute neurovascular change.
assessMonitor: Pain, mobility, incision, neurovascular status, transfer safety, and adherence to prescribed precautions.
interventions: Use ordered assistive devices and positioning; coordinate PT/OT recommendations.
medicationSafety: Monitor opioid/sedative effects that increase fall risk; follow ordered VTE prophylaxis safely.
teaching: Use only the movement restrictions prescribed for the specific surgical approach.
delegationScope: Transfers may be delegated to trained staff within the care plan; assessment of new pain/deformity requires licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Teaching posterior-approach precautions to every hip-replacement patient regardless of approach.
oneLinePearl: Hip precautions are approach-specific, not universal.
sourceBasis: AAOS total hip replacement recovery principles

title: Knee Arthroplasty Recovery: Move Safely, Watch for VTE and Infection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Early mobility, pain control, prescribed exercises, and VTE/infection surveillance are central after knee arthroplasty. New calf swelling, chest symptoms, fever, or draining erythematous incision requires escalation.
recognize: Expected postoperative pain/swelling should gradually improve with the care plan.
Unilateral calf swelling, sudden dyspnea, chest pain, or rapidly increasing wound drainage is not routine recovery.
priorities: Mobilize according to PT/OT and surgical orders while maintaining fall precautions.
Escalate VTE, PE, infection, or neurovascular warning signs.
assessMonitor: Pain, mobility, wound, temperature, limb swelling, neurovascular status, respiratory symptoms.
interventions: Support prescribed ROM, ambulation, icing/elevation if ordered, and prophylaxis adherence.
medicationSafety: Balance analgesia with fall/respiratory risk and reinforce anticoagulant precautions when prescribed.
teaching: Complete prescribed exercises and report clot/infection symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Routine ambulation may be delegated per plan; abnormal findings require licensed reassessment.
examTrap: Keeping the patient on bed rest to prevent pain.
oneLinePearl: After knee replacement, safe movement prevents complications.
sourceBasis: AAOS total knee replacement recovery principles

title: Osteoporosis Safety: Prevent the Next Fracture
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Osteoporosis care is not only medication adherence; fracture prevention also requires fall-risk reduction, strength/balance activity, adequate calcium/vitamin D intake, and prompt evaluation after low-trauma fractures.
recognize: Prior fragility fracture strongly predicts future fracture risk.
Sedatives, orthostasis, vision impairment, unsafe footwear, and home hazards compound skeletal risk.
priorities: Address fall risks and reinforce the prescribed bone-health plan.
Report new severe back/hip pain after minor trauma because occult fracture is possible.
assessMonitor: Falls, mobility, pain, adherence, nutrition, vitamin D/calcium plan, and medication adverse effects.
interventions: Promote safe weight-bearing/balance exercise and home hazard reduction as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Bisphosphonates, denosumab, and other therapies have product-specific administration and monitoring rules; reinforce the prescribed regimen accurately.
redFlags: Severe back pain after minor trauma
teaching: Preventing falls is part of osteoporosis treatment.
delegationScope: Environmental safety tasks may be delegated; fracture-risk teaching and abnormal symptom escalation remain licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Focusing only on calcium supplements while ignoring repeated falls.
oneLinePearl: Bone strength matters, but fall prevention prevents fractures today.
sourceBasis: Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation patient-care principles

title: Traction Safety: Keep the Line of Pull Intact
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Effective traction depends on continuous prescribed alignment and unobstructed weights. Do not remove or rest weights unless specifically ordered.
recognize: Ropes should move freely in pulleys and weights should hang without touching the floor or bed.
Increasing pain, skin breakdown, numbness, or loss of alignment requires reassessment.
priorities: Maintain body alignment and the prescribed line of pull.
Escalate neurovascular compromise or equipment failure.
assessMonitor: Neurovascular status, skin/pressure points, pin sites if skeletal traction, alignment, rope/pulley function.
interventions: Reposition within the prescribed system and protect skin; maintain pin care per protocol.
medicationSafety: Monitor analgesic effects without masking neurovascular deterioration.
teaching: Do not alter weights or traction equipment.
delegationScope: Basic comfort care may be delegated; traction adjustments require authorized trained personnel.
examTrap: Removing weights briefly to improve comfort.
oneLinePearl: Traction works only when the pull stays continuous and aligned.

title: Amputation Recovery: Protect the Residual Limb and Mobility
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: After amputation, wound healing, contracture prevention, positioning, mobility, pain management, and psychosocial support all affect prosthetic readiness and independence.
recognize: Residual-limb infection, skin breakdown, edema, severe phantom pain, or flexion contracture can delay rehabilitation.
Phantom limb sensations are common and should be acknowledged rather than dismissed.
priorities: Protect the incision/residual limb and follow positioning/ROM guidance to prevent contractures.
Escalate infection, ischemia, uncontrolled pain, or acute mood/safety concerns.
assessMonitor: Incision, edema, pain, skin, ROM, coping, mobility, and fall risk.
interventions: Support prescribed wrapping/shrinker use, ROM, transfers, and PT/OT plan.
medicationSafety: Monitor analgesics and neuropathic-pain agents for sedation/fall risk.
teaching: Inspect the residual limb daily and follow prosthetic-team skin-care instructions.
delegationScope: Routine hygiene may be delegated; wound/skin changes and psychosocial safety findings require licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Keeping the hip/knee flexed for prolonged comfort and promoting contracture.
oneLinePearl: Protect the limb today so mobility is possible tomorrow.

title: Low Back Pain: Screen for Cauda Equina and Other Red Flags
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Most acute low back pain is not emergent, but new urinary retention/incontinence, saddle anesthesia, progressive bilateral weakness, fever, cancer history, major trauma, or severe neurologic deficit requires urgent escalation.
recognize: Cauda equina syndrome can present with saddle sensory loss, bladder/bowel dysfunction, and progressive lower-extremity weakness.
Fever/immunosuppression raises concern for spinal infection; trauma/osteoporosis raises fracture risk.
priorities: Escalate neurologic red flags promptly rather than treating them as routine musculoskeletal pain.
Maintain fall precautions if weakness or sensory loss is present.
assessMonitor: Motor/sensory changes, bladder/bowel function, gait, pain pattern, fever, trauma and cancer/infection risk factors.
interventions: Support ordered analgesia and safe mobility while urgent evaluation proceeds when red flags exist.
medicationSafety: Sedating analgesics can obscure neurologic changes and increase fall risk; reassess function.
teaching: Seek urgent care for new bladder/bowel dysfunction, saddle numbness, or progressive weakness.
delegationScope: Routine mobility assistance may be delegated; neurologic red-flag assessment/escalation is licensed work.
examTrap: Giving another PRN analgesic and waiting despite new urinary retention and saddle numbness.
oneLinePearl: Back pain plus bladder, bowel, saddle, or progressive weakness is an emergency pattern.
sourceBasis: American College of Radiology low-back red-flag principles

title: Rhabdomyolysis: Dark Urine Plus Muscle Injury Is a Renal Threat
bottomLine: Rhabdomyolysis releases muscle contents that can cause hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury. Muscle pain/weakness, dark urine, trauma/immobility, heat illness, seizures, or medication triggers require prompt evaluation and trending.
recognize: Dark tea-colored urine after muscle injury is concerning but may be absent.
Hyperkalemia and rising creatinine are dangerous complications.
priorities: Escalate suspected rhabdomyolysis and monitor cardiac/renal status as ordered.
Support prescribed fluids and avoid nephrotoxic exposures when directed.
assessMonitor: Urine output/color, CK, creatinine, potassium, ECG/rhythm, hydration, pain/weakness.
interventions: Administer ordered IV fluids and monitor response; treat hyperkalemia per protocol/order.
medicationSafety: Review statins and other possible contributors; do not stop prescribed drugs independently unless an emergency protocol directs it.
teaching: Report severe muscle pain/weakness with dark urine, especially after heat injury, prolonged immobility, or medication changes.
delegationScope: Urine measurement may be delegated; interpretation of trends and escalation remain licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Treating dark urine as simple dehydration without considering muscle injury.
oneLinePearl: Muscle breakdown can become a kidney and potassium emergency.

title: Rehabilitation Transfers: Protect Function Without Creating a Fall
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Safe rehabilitation transfers require matching assistance level, device, footwear, cognition, weight-bearing status, and fatigue to the patient's current function—not yesterday's function.
recognize: Orthostasis, new weakness, sedation, pain, confusion, or fatigue can suddenly increase transfer risk.
A gait belt or device is only safe when used correctly and when not contraindicated.
priorities: Verify weight-bearing/activity orders and the current assistance level before transfer.
Stop and reassess if the patient becomes dizzy, buckles, or cannot follow commands safely.
assessMonitor: Strength, balance, cognition, orthostasis, pain, fatigue, footwear, lines/tubes, prescribed assistive device.
interventions: Use trained assistance, clear the environment, lock equipment, and follow PT/OT transfer technique.
medicationSafety: Opioids, sedatives, antihypertensives, and hypoglycemics can increase fall risk; correlate symptoms with medication timing.
teaching: Ask for help rather than attempting a transfer above the prescribed assistance level.
delegationScope: Transfers may be delegated to trained staff when stable and within the care plan; changes in functional status require licensed reassessment.
examTrap: Using the same transfer plan despite new dizziness and weakness.
oneLinePearl: Transfer safety depends on how the patient is functioning now.
